before: You can see the same move in a dramatized scene from the movie A Beautiful Day in the Neighborhood. Lloyd, a reporter, tells Mr. Rogers, "I can't imagine it was easy… growing up with you as a father." He doesn't collapse under that or fight it, but he does answer what's worth answering in it. He tells Lloyd that until recently his oldest son never told people about his dad, and his youngest "genuinely tested" him. Eventually he and his youngest found their way, and now he's very proud of both his sons. Then he says, "But you are right, Lloyd. It couldn't have been easy on them. Thank you. Thank you for that perspective." Like the two truths at bedtime, a true complaint and real love don't cancel each other out, so you can take the true part without giving up your love or defending yourself.

brief:
- the guide: "Also notice what happens between the internal positions." In the article's words: notice what goes on between the parts of you, inside, not only between you and your little one out loud.
- the guide: "If distrust is followed by accusation, the younger state may learn that love remains available only while it is received correctly." So if their "I don't believe you" gets answered with an accusation, your little one can learn that your love is only there as long as they take it the right way.
- the guide: "The resentful voice and the vow-making voice may be the same position, different positions, or a blend." In plain words: the part of you that resents them for not believing you, and the part that wants to promise them things, may be one part, two parts, or a mix. The promise is the next section's subject, so don't call it a vow or explain it here.
- the guide: "Don't merge them simply because both appear through the grown-up mind." Don't lump them together just because both talk in your grown-up voice.
- the article already has, earlier in this section: "try not to turn \"But I love you\" into a line you say on cue, because then it can brush the anger off". Don't repeat that point.
